tasks.request: Reconcile six months of bank statements, categorize expenses, and prepare a business tax filing package.
responseEvidence:
I checked the catalog first, then read both definitions in full. Here's where things stand.

## No playbook covers this

Your Owenloop catalog publishes exactly two workflows:

| Workflow | Scope | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **code-delivery** | Implement/test/review an approved change in a software repo | No |
| **library-build** | Research a topic, gather sources, synthesize a knowledge library | No |

Both explicitly list the *other* as "not for" — they're a narrow pair aimed at software delivery and research curation. Neither has any bookkeeping, ledger, reconciliation, or tax capability.

I also considered compiling a bespoke composite from existing playbooks. That's only appropriate when two catalog playbooks genuinely cover most of the work and leave one coherent gap. Here they'd cover *none* of it — reconciliation, categorization, and tax package assembly would all be the "gap." That's not a composite, it's freelancing with extra steps, so I didn't do it.

## Why I'm not just doing it inline

Two reasons, and the second is the important one:

1. **No access.** In this session I have no file, spreadsheet, or system tools — only the Owenloop control plane. I can't open a statement, let alone six months of them across your accounts.

2. **This is the wrong task to improvise on.** A tax filing package is a legally attested document. Categorized expenses I invented, or reconciliations I couldn't tie to real statement balances, would look completely finished and be entirely wrong — and you'd sign your name to it. Fabricated progress here has real consequences with the IRS. I'd rather hand you nothing than hand you a confident, unfounded return.

## What would actually move this forward

**Option A — publish a bookkeeping playbook.** This is the durable fix. A `books-close` or `tax-package` workflow with real crews would let you run this every quarter instead of re-litigating it. The natural shape:

- Ingest statements per account, per month
- Reconcile each period against opening/closing balances, flag unmatched items
- Categorize transactions to a chart of accounts, with an escalation path for ambiguous ones
- Assemble the filing package, gated on your review
- Human approval gate before anything is treated as final

If you want, I'll draft that definition for you to review and publish.

**Option B — a one-off ephemeral run.** Appropriate for a genuine single instance. But it only helps if the work can actually be executed against your real data — I'd still need the statements reachable by tooling. If they're PDFs in a folder or exports from a bank/accounting system, tell me where and how they're accessible.

**Option C — this may not belong in an agent loop at all.** Worth saying plainly: a business return usually wants a CPA who can sign it and carries liability for it. Automation is great at the reconciliation and categorization grind underneath. The filing itself is a different kind of decision.

## To get started, I'd need

- Which accounts, and the exact six-month window (calendar H1 2026? fiscal year?)
- Entity type — sole prop, LLC, S-corp, partnership — this drives the whole package
- Where the statements live and how they're accessible
- Your existing chart of accounts, or whether one needs building
- Whether a CPA is in the loop, and at which point

Tell me which option you want and I'll take the next step. If it's Option A, I'll start on the playbook draft now.

tasks.request: Compare medical providers, verify insurance coverage, schedule an appointment, and arrange transportation.
responseEvidence:
I checked the catalog first, and inspected both published playbooks. Here's where things stand.

## The catalog doesn't cover this

Your published workflows are:

| Workflow | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **code-delivery** | Implement/test/review an approved change in a software repo |
| **library-build** | Research a topic and synthesize a sourced knowledge library |

Neither serves any of the four things you asked for. This isn't a partial fit I can stretch — provider comparison, insurance verification, appointment booking, and ride arrangement share no capability with either playbook. I also don't have a crew that serves those capabilities, so I'm not going to compile a bespoke composite out of two playbooks that each contribute nothing, and I'm not going to open a run and report progress I didn't actually make.

## What genuinely blocks each step

Three of the four steps aren't research problems — they're real-world transactions that commit you to something, and each needs an access path I don't have:

- **Verify insurance coverage** — requires authenticated access to your member portal or a call to your insurer with your member ID and group number. Coverage quotes from any other source aren't reliable enough to schedule against.
- **Schedule an appointment** — requires booking authority on your behalf, plus a confirmed provider and a real time slot.
- **Arrange transportation** — requires an account with a ride service or a medical transport benefit, and it can't be sequenced until the appointment time is locked.

The dependency also matters: verify coverage *before* booking, and book *before* arranging the ride. Doing these out of order is how people end up with a surprise bill or a ride to a cancelled slot.

## What I can actually do now

**Provider comparison** is the one piece that's genuinely research, and `library-build` could do a real version of it — a sourced comparison of candidate providers with credentials, hospital affiliations, subspecialty focus, and patient-experience signals. That's an honest use of the playbook, not a stretch.

To start it I'd need from you:

1. **Specialty or condition** — what kind of provider
2. **Geography** — city or ZIP, and how far you're willing to travel
3. **Insurer and plan name** — so the comparison can flag network status as a research signal (still to be confirmed with the insurer directly, not treated as verified)
4. Any constraints that matter — hospital system preference, telehealth vs. in-person, language, accessibility

Say the word and I'll start that run. For the other three steps, the cleanest path is that I produce a call-ready packet — the questions to ask your insurer, the CPT/diagnosis details to quote, and a booking-and-ride checklist sequenced correctly — and you make the two calls that need your identity and authority. If you'd rather I flag this as a catalog gap worth a real workflow, that's the durable fix, since this is clearly a recurring need.

tasks.request: Investigate a legacy service and produce a migration brief with evidence and recommended next steps.
responseEvidence:
I checked the catalog and inspected both playbooks. Here's where things stand.

**Recommended playbook: `library-build`**

It's the right shape for this request: research a subject across subtopics, acquire and cite source artifacts, and synthesize them into a linked, evidence-backed body of work. A migration brief is exactly that — findings on the current service, dependency and risk evidence, and a synthesized set of recommendations.

**Not `code-delivery`** — it's scoped to delivering an *already approved* repository change, and its definition explicitly excludes research and curation work. Your brief is what would precede an approved change, not the change itself.

I also considered compiling a bespoke composite of the two playbooks, but that's only warranted when two *compatible* playbooks combine cleanly. These two explicitly disclaim each other's territory, so a composite would be forced. One playbook fits, and I'd rather run it straight.

**Before I start the run, I need three things I can't invent for you:**

1. **Which legacy service?** A name, repo, or system identifier. "A legacy service" won't survive contact with the crews — they'd produce a generic essay instead of evidence about your system.
2. **Migrating to what?** Even a rough target (new platform, language, managed service, or "target undecided — evaluate options") changes whether this is an evaluation brief or a path-to-target brief.
3. **What decision does the brief serve, and for whom?** An exec go/no-go read differently than an engineering sequencing plan. Any hard constraints — deadlines, compliance, freeze windows — are useful here too.

If you have access notes to point at (repo paths, runbooks, dashboards, incident history), send those along and I'll fold them into the run scope so the evidence is drawn from your material rather than assembled from general knowledge.

Give me those and I'll open the `library-build` run scoped to your service, then monitor it and relay any gates, worker questions, or receipts back to you as they come up.

tasks.request: Collect competitor material and turn it into a launch-readiness brief for a software product.
responseEvidence:
I read the catalog and inspected both definitions. Here's where things stand before I start anything.

**What fits:** `library-build` — "research a topic across subtopics, acquire source and media artifacts, and synthesize a linked knowledge library." That squarely covers the collect-competitor-material half, and its synthesis step is the right vehicle for the brief.

**What doesn't:** `code-delivery` is for implementing an approved change in an existing repo, and its definition explicitly lists "research and curate a topical media or knowledge library" under *notFor*. The word "software" in your request describes the *subject* of the brief, not the work to be done — there's no code to ship here. So it's not a second compatible playbook, which means this is a single-playbook job, not a composite. I'm not going to manufacture a two-workflow plan to justify a fancier route.

**One caveat to set expectations:** `library-build` outputs a linked knowledge library. A launch-readiness brief is a narrower, more opinionated artifact. I can scope that framing into the topic so the synthesis lands as a brief, but the deliverable will carry library DNA — sourced, subtopic-organized, citation-linked. If you need a formal go/no-go memo with sign-off owners, that shaping may need a pass afterward.

**What I need from you before starting.** The topic input is a single free-text scope, and "a software product" isn't researchable as written. Starting a run on an undefined subject would burn crew effort and produce material you'd reject. Three things:

1. **The product** — name, and one line on what it does and who buys it.
2. **The competitors** — a named set, or tell me to let the crew derive the set and I'll scope that in.
3. **Launch-readiness against what** — the decisions this brief informs. Pricing position? Feature gaps? Messaging differentiation? Timing? "Readiness" means different research without a criterion.

If it's useful, a workable topic string would read something like: *"Competitive landscape for [product], a [category] tool for [buyer]. Cover [competitors] across positioning, pricing, feature coverage, and go-to-market motion. Synthesize into a launch-readiness assessment identifying gaps and risks against [launch date]."*

Send me those three and I'll start the run immediately, then park on `wake` and relay any gates or worker asks as they come. If you'd rather I proceed with a deliberately broad scope and let the crew narrow the competitor set itself, say so and I'll launch on that basis — just know the first synthesis will be wider and less decision-ready.
